analysis.one_liner: Gives long-term residents brought here as children a path to permanent legal status through school, work, or military service.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on December 4, 2025 with one Republican cosponsor and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Dream Act of 2025 would let certain people who came to the United States as children, have lived here for years, and stay in school, work, or serve in the military apply to stay legally. They would first get an eight-year conditional green card, then a permanent one if they finish college or two years of it, serve two years in the military, or work at least three years. The bill also blocks the deportation of people who appear eligible while they apply, and bars the government from using application information to deport them.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are Dreamers: people who entered the US before age 18 and have lived here continuously for at least four years, pass criminal and security background checks, and meet an education, work, or military-service condition. For them, the bill converts life under threat of deportation into a documented, stable status, with work permits, protection from removal while applying, a guarantee that their application information will not be used to deport them, and, after eight years of conditional status, a permanent green card. Communities, families, and employers who depend on these workers also benefit from the stability the bill creates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Long-term residents brought here as children

how_it_helps.text: The Department of Homeland Security must cancel the deportation of, and grant eight-year conditional permanent residence to, people who entered the US under age 18, have lived here continuously for at least four years, pass criminal and security checks, and are in school, have a high school diploma or GED, are admitted to college, or have served in the military [S2].

After eight years in conditional status, people qualify for full green cards by completing a college degree or two years of college, serving two years in the military, or working at least three of the years they held work authorization, with hardship exceptions for disability, full-time caregiving, or extreme hardship to a US-citizen or green-card spouse, parent, or child [S2].

While applications are pending, people who appear eligible cannot be deported, and school-age children who meet the basic requirements get a stay of removal and a work permit; people granted conditional status count as lawfully present for naturalization purposes later [S2].

Information in applications and DACA requests cannot be used for immigration enforcement or referred to ICE or Border Protection, with a narrow exception for national security and felony investigations, and violators face fines up to $10,000 [S2].

There is no cap on how many people can qualify, and the Secretary must publish rules within 90 days of enactment so eligible people can apply affirmatively without first being placed in removal proceedings; very poor applicants, minors, homeless youth, people with chronic disabilities, and those with large medical debt can have fees waived [S2].

analysis.who_pays: No direct taxpayer cost appears in the bill: applicants pay fees set to match processing costs, though very low-income applicants can be exempted. The broader costs are borne by applicants themselves — fees, background checks, medical exams, and a heavy documentation burden — and by the immigration enforcement system, which would forgo removing people who qualify. Opponents bear a political cost in the sense that the bill legalizes people who entered without authorization; the text does not quantify any fiscal cost.

drawbacks.text: The status is conditional and can be terminated if a person stops meeting the school, work, or military requirements; the Secretary must give notice and a hearing first, but people who fall out of status return to whatever immigration status they had before, with deportation exposure restored [S2].

Eligibility is narrow: it covers people who entered before age 18 and have been continuously present for at least four years, with criminal bars (no offense punishable by more than a year, or three offenses totaling 90 days or more), required background checks, medical exams, and Selective Service registration where applicable [S2].

It does not grant citizenship: a person cannot naturalize while in conditional status, and full permanent residence requires a college degree, two years of military service, or three years of mostly continuous employment, with only limited hardship exceptions for disability, caregiving, or extreme hardship to a US-citizen or green-card family member [S2].

The documentation burden is heavy: applicants must prove identity, age at entry, and years of continuous presence with extensive records — employment, school, rent, bank, and tax records — or sworn affidavits from unrelated people, which many long-term residents will struggle to produce [S2].

The Secretary may charge application fees at both stages, exempting only very low-income applicants (under 150% of poverty) facing specific hardships such as homelessness, disability, foster care, or large medical debt [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the bill helps a specific, vulnerable group of long-term residents at little direct cost to anyone else: applicants pay processing fees, must pass background checks, meet education, work, or military conditions, and hold only conditional status for eight years before qualifying for full permanent residence. The strongest good-faith objections are that it rewards unlawful entry and that its school, work, and documentation requirements will exclude some people who came here as children. It is a narrower and more conditional path than a simple amnesty, but it is also not a guaranteed one: status can lapse or be terminated, and people who fall out of status return to deportation exposure.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Durbin introduced it on December 4, 2025, and instead of a debate or a vote it was read twice and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 4, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S4].
No committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind appears in the record after the referral [S4].
Only one senator, Republican Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, cosponsored the bill with lead sponsor Dick Durbin [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet from the bill itself; because it has only been referred to committee, the situation it would change remains exactly as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill is led by a Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor out of 55 Senate Republicans, and no floor or committee vote has occurred to show how the parties line up.

industries.industry: Employers in agriculture, construction, and hospitality that rely on long-term immigrant workers
industries.note: Legal status keeps experienced workers employed and off the deportation rolls, stabilizing workforces that depend on immigrant labor. Workers' gain and employers' gain here run in the same direction.
Admission to or enrollment in higher education qualifies people for status, which would add students to higher-education rolls. The benefit is shared with the students themselves.

People who appear eligible cannot be removed and their information cannot be referred to ICE or Border Protection, shrinking the population subject to detention and removal. Fewer detainees means less business for detention and enforcement operations.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress is still in session, but the bill's path is narrow. It arrived late in the first session with one Republican cosponsor and has drawn no committee action; immigration bills of this kind typically need either a Senate floor deal or a ride on a larger must-pass package. Unless it picks up substantial Republican support or is attached to broader legislation, the most likely outcome is that it sits in the Judiciary Committee until the Congress ends.
